{{Short description|Tree in set theory}}
[[File:Aronszajn tree.svg|thumb|upright=1.25|A portion of a ''special'' Aronszajn tree]]
In [[set theory]], an '''Aronszajn tree''' is a [[tree (set theory)|tree]] of uncountable height with no uncountable branches and no uncountable levels. For example, every [[Suslin tree]] is an Aronszajn tree. More generally, for a [[Cardinal number|cardinal]] ''κ'', a '''''κ''-Aronszajn tree''' is a tree of height ''κ'' in which all levels have size less than ''κ'' and all branches have height less than ''κ'' (so Aronszajn trees are the same as <math>\aleph_1</math>-Aronszajn trees). They are named for [[Nachman Aronszajn]], who constructed an Aronszajn tree in 1934; his construction was described by {{harvtxt|Kurepa|1935}}. 

A cardinal ''κ'' for which no ''κ''-Aronszajn trees exist is said to have the '''tree property'''
(sometimes the condition that ''κ'' is regular and uncountable is included).

==Existence of &kappa;-Aronszajn trees==
[[Kőnig's lemma]]  states that <math>\aleph_0</math>-Aronszajn trees do not exist.

The existence of Aronszajn trees (<math>=\aleph_1</math>-Aronszajn trees) was proven by [[Nachman Aronszajn]], and implies that the analogue of [[Kőnig's lemma]] does not hold for uncountable trees.

The existence of <math>\aleph_2</math>-Aronszajn trees is undecidable in ZFC: more precisely, the [[continuum hypothesis]] implies the existence of an <math>\aleph_2</math>-Aronszajn tree, and Mitchell and Silver showed that it is [[consistent]] (relative to the existence of a [[weakly compact cardinal]]) that no <math>\aleph_2</math>-Aronszajn trees exist.

[[Ronald Jensen|Jensen]] proved that [[V&nbsp;=&nbsp;L]] implies that there is a ''κ''-Aronszajn tree (in fact a ''κ''-[[Suslin tree]]) for every infinite successor cardinal&nbsp;''κ''.

{{harvtxt|Cummings|Foreman|1998}} showed (using a large cardinal axiom) that it is consistent that no <math>\aleph_n</math>-Aronszajn trees exist for any finite ''n'' other than&nbsp;1.

If ''κ'' is weakly compact then no ''κ''-Aronszajn trees exist. Conversely, if ''κ'' is [[inaccessible cardinal|inaccessible]] and no ''κ''-Aronszajn trees exist, then ''κ'' is weakly compact.

==Special Aronszajn trees==
An Aronszajn tree is called '''special''' if there is a function ''f'' from the tree to the rationals so that
''f''(''x'')&nbsp;<&nbsp;''f''(''y'') whenever ''x''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''y''. [[Martin's axiom]] MA(<math>\aleph_1</math>) implies that all Aronszajn trees are special, a proposition sometimes abbreviated by '''EATS'''. The stronger [[proper forcing axiom]] implies the stronger statement that for any two Aronszajn trees  there is a [[club set]] of levels such that the restrictions of the trees to this set of levels are isomorphic, which says that in some sense any two Aronszajn trees are essentially isomorphic  {{harv|Abraham|Shelah|1985}}. On the other hand, it is consistent that non-special Aronszajn trees exist, and this is also consistent with the [[generalized continuum hypothesis]] plus [[Suslin hypothesis|Suslin's hypothesis]] {{harv|Schlindwein|1994}}.

==Construction of a special Aronszajn tree==

A special Aronszajn tree can be constructed as follows. 

The elements of the tree are certain well-ordered sets of rational numbers with supremum that is rational or −∞.  If ''x'' and ''y'' are two of these sets then we define ''x''&nbsp;&le;&nbsp;''y'' (in the tree order) to mean that ''x'' is an initial segment of the ordered set&nbsp;''y''. For each countable ordinal α we write ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> for the elements of the tree of level α, so that the elements of ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> are certain sets of rationals with order type α. The special Aronszajn tree ''T'' is the union of the sets ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> for all countable α. 

We construct the countable levels ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> by transfinite induction on α as follows starting with the empty set as ''U''<sub>''0''</sub>:

*If ''α''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 is a successor then ''U''<sub>''α''+1</sub> consists of all extensions of a sequence ''x'' in ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> by a rational greater than sup ''x''. ''U''<sub>''α''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1</sub> is countable as it consists of countably many extensions of each of the countably many elements in ''U''<sub>''α''</sub>.
*If ''α'' is a limit then let ''T''<sub>''α''</sub> be the tree of all points of level less than ''α''. For each ''x'' in ''T''<sub>''α''</sub> and for each rational number ''q'' greater than sup ''x'', choose a level ''α'' branch of ''T''<sub>''α''</sub> containing ''x'' with supremum ''q''. Then ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> consists of these branches. ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> is countable as it consists of countably many branches for each of the countably many elements in ''T''<sub>''α''</sub>.

The function ''f''(''x'') =&nbsp;sup&nbsp;''x'' is rational or −∞, and has the property that if ''x''&nbsp;<&nbsp;''y'' then ''f''(''x'')&nbsp;<&nbsp;''f''(''y''). Any branch in ''T'' is countable as ''f'' maps branches injectively to −∞ and the rationals. ''T'' is uncountable as it has a non-empty level ''U''<sub>''α''</sub> for each countable ordinal ''α'' which make up the [[first uncountable ordinal]]. This proves that ''T'' is a special Aronszajn tree.

This construction can be used to construct ''κ''-Aronszajn trees whenever ''κ'' is a successor of a regular cardinal and the generalized continuum hypothesis holds, by replacing the rational numbers by a more general [[η set|''η'' set]].
